before: As the citizen of a free state, and a member of the supreme power, by birth, however weak may be the influence of my single vote in public affairs, the right of giving that vote is sufficient to impose on me the duty of making those affairs my study, thinking myself happy in discussing the various forms of government, to find every day new reasons for admiring that of my own country !
after: Although my birth in a free polity makes me one of its citizens and a participant in its highest authority, a single ballot has little weight. The entitlement to cast it nevertheless obliges me to learn about public matters. I count myself fortunate to study arrangements for governing and discover afresh each day why my homeland’s constitution deserves my admiration!

before: THE most ancient of all societies, and the only natural one, is that of a family. And even in this, children are no longer connected with their father, than while they stand in need of his assistance. When this becomes needless, the natural tie is of course dissolved, the children are exempted from the obedience they owe their father, and the father is equally so from the solicitude due from him to his children; both assume a state of independence respecting each other. They may continue, indeed, to live together afterwards; but their connection, in such a case, is no longer natural, but voluntary; and even the family union is then maintained by mutual convention.
after: The household is humanity’s earliest association and the sole bond founded in nature. Even there, a child remains connected to his father only while he needs the father’s support. Once that dependence disappears, nature’s tie ends: the child no longer owes obedience, and the father no longer owes care. Each stands independently. They may choose to continue living together, but what keeps them together then is not nature. Their family remains united by a mutual agreement.

before: Aristotle was right as to the fact, but mistook the effect for the cause. Nothing is more certain, than that every man born in slavery is born to be a slave. In such a state, men lose even the desire of freedom, and prefer subjection, as the companions of Ulysses did their brutality. If there are any slaves, therefore, by nature, it is because they are slaves contrary to nature. Power first made slaves, and cowardice hath perpetuated them.
after: Aristotle described the situation correctly but reversed cause and result. Someone entering life already enslaved is indeed born into that condition. People in bondage may even lose the wish to be free and favor their subjection, as Ulysses’ companions preferred their transformation into beasts. Any people who appear enslaved by nature must, then, have first been enslaved against nature. Violence created servitude; fear kept it in place.

before: I have said nothing of king Adam, or the emperor Noah, father of three monarchs, who, like the children of Saturn, as some have imagined them to be, divided the world among them. I hope my moderation also in this respect will be esteemed some merit; for, as I am descended in a right line from one of these princes, and probably from the eldest branch of the family, how do I know, that, by a regular deduction of my descent, I might not find myself the legitimate heir to universal monarchy? Be this, however, as it may, it cannot be denied, that Adam had as good a title to the sovereignty of the world, when he was the only person in it, as Robinson Crusoe had to that of his island under the same circumstances. A very great conveniency also attended their government, in that the monarch might rest securely on his throne, without fear of wars, conspiracies, or rebellion.
after: Nor have I discussed Adam the king and Noah the emperor, whose three sons were said to divide the earth among themselves, like Saturn’s children in one account. I hope my restraint here earns some credit. I descend in a straight line from one of these rulers, perhaps through the family’s eldest branch. A complete genealogy might even show that I am the rightful heir to world monarchy. Whatever one makes of that claim, when Adam was its only inhabitant he had as valid a title to rule the whole earth as Robinson Crusoe had to govern his island in the same situation. Their rule had another great advantage: each monarch could sit safely, free of wars, plots, or rebellion.

before: THE strongest is not strong enough to continue always master, unless he transforms his power into a right of command, and obedience into a duty. Hence is deduced the right of the strongest; a right taken ironically in appearance, and laid down as an established principle in reality. But will this term never be rightly explained? Force, in the simplest sense, is a physical power; nor can I see what morality can result from its effects. To yield to superior force is an act of necessity, not of the will; at most it is but an act of prudence. And in what sense can this be called a duty?
after: Strength alone cannot secure permanent rule. The powerful man must recast his force as a legitimate command, and make compliance seem an obligation. That is the source of the so-called entitlement of the strongest: on the surface a joke, yet asserted as a real principle. Can anyone ever explain this phrase sensibly? Force at bottom is bodily power; I cannot see how moral authority follows from it. Yielding to greater force is compelled by necessity, not chosen freely. At most, submission is cautious self-preservation. Why call that a duty?

before: If an individual, says Grotius, can alienate his liberty, and become the slave of a master, why may not a whole people collectively alienate theirs, and become subject to a king? This proposition, however, contains some equivocal terms, which require explanation, but I shall confine myself to that of alienate. Whatever is alienated must be disposed of, either by gift or sale. Now a man who becomes the slave of another doth not give himself away, but sells himself, at least for his subsistence; but why should a whole people sell themselves? So far is a king from furnishing his subjects subsistence, that they maintain him; and, as our friend Rabelais says, A king doth not live on a little. Can subjects be supposed to give away their liberty, on condition that the receiver shall take their property along with it? After this, I really cannot see any thing they have left.
after: Grotius asks whether one individual may bargain away liberty and become another’s slave, and whether a people together may similarly place themselves beneath a king. His terms need clarification; I will address only “alienate.” Disposing of something means either giving it away or selling it. A man who enters slavery does not give himself as a present. He trades himself, if only for the means to survive. What could induce an entire population to make such a sale? A ruler does not feed his people; they pay for his livelihood. Rabelais jokes that a king needs more than a little sustenance. Would citizens surrender their freedom while granting the recipient their goods as well? After that exchange, what would be left in their possession?

before: War is not, therefore, any relation between man and man, but a relation between state and state, in which individuals are enemies only accidentally, not as men, or even as citizens, but as soldiers; not as members of their particular community, but as its defenders. In short, a state can have for its enemy nothing but a state, not men; as between things essentially different, there can be no common relation.
after: War takes place between organized polities; it is not a private quarrel among human beings. A person from the other side is an enemy only by accident of military role—not through his humanity or even his civic identity, but because he bears arms to defend his community. Thus the opposing party is a state, not individual people; entities that differ in kind have no shared relation as enemies.

before: The foreigner, whether a sovereign, an individual or a people, who plunders, kills, or takes prisoner a subject, without declaring war against his prince, is not an enemy, but a robber. Even in a time of war, a just prince may make himself master, in an enemy's country, of whatever belongs to the public, but he will respect the persons and private properties of individuals; he will respect those rights on which his own are founded. The design of war being the destruction of an hostile state, we have a right to kill its defenders, while they are in arms; but as, in laying down their arms, they cease to be enemies, or instruments of hostility, they become, in that case, mere men, and we have not the least right to murder them. It is sometimes possible effectually to destroy a state, without killing even one of its members; now war cannot confer any right or privilege, which is not necessary to accomplish its end and design. It is true, these are not the principles of Grotius, nor are they founded on the authority of the poets; but they are such as are deduced from the nature of things, and are founded on reason.
after: If a foreign ruler, person, or nation attacks one of our subjects—looting, killing, or capturing him—without proclaiming war against the prince, that is banditry, not warfare. Even in a declared conflict, a just ruler may seize public property in enemy territory while leaving private persons and their possessions unharmed, respecting the same rights that ground his own. War aims to defeat the hostile state, so its defenders may be killed while they remain armed. Once they put down weapons, they are no longer enemies or instruments of battle but ordinary people; there is no license to murder them. A state might be brought down without a single inhabitant killed. War grants no entitlement beyond what its purpose requires. These propositions do not come from Grotius or poetic authority; they arise from the nature of the case and from reason.

before: With regard to the right of conquest, it has no other foundation than that of force, the law of the strongest. But, if war doth not give the victor a right to massacre the vanquished, this pretended right, which does not exist, cannot be the foundation of a right to enslave them. If we have no right to kill an enemy, unless we cannot by force reduce him to slavery, our right to make him a slave never can be founded on our right to kill him. It is, therefore, an iniquitous bargain, to make him purchase, at the expence of liberty, a life, which we have no right to take away. In establishing thus a right of life and death over others, on that of enslaving them; and, on the other hand, a right of enslaving them on that of life and death, we certainly fall into the absurdity of reasoning in a circle.
after: Conquest claims no legitimacy beyond superior force. Since a victor has no right to slaughter the defeated, this imagined permission cannot support a power to enslave them either. If killing an enemy is justified only when he cannot be subdued into bondage, then a right to enslave cannot rest on a right to kill. It is unjust to demand a person’s freedom as payment for sparing a life that we had no entitlement to take. To derive authority over life and death from enslavement, while justifying enslavement through that same authority, is circular reasoning.
